# Scene Blocking

## Purpose
Place characters and action in concrete space: who stands where, who moves
where and when, who looks at whom, what their hands are doing — and establish
the axes that all coverage must respect.

## Use When
- Breaking down a scene before shot planning.
- A scene's coverage feels spatially confused or reverses don't cut.
- Script revisions change who is present or how the action flows.

## Inputs
- `production/scenes/<SC_ID>/scene.yaml` (beats, entities, structural function).
- `production/locations/<LOC_ID>/map.yaml` (plan, zones, angles, north).
- Character and prop bibles for physicality and object handling.

## Process
1. Anchor the scene to plan coordinates: assign each character a start
   position and orientation on the location map, in a named zone.
2. Establish stage geography for the audience: decide what the establishing
   view must show so later close coverage stays legible.
3. Block movement per beat: path, trigger (line or event), and end position;
   movement without dramatic motivation is cut, not decorated.
4. Define eyelines: who looks at whom or what per beat, with plan direction,
   including objects and off-screen points of attention.
5. Give every character business — physical activity that expresses state
   (packing the suitcase, gripping the rail) — tied to props from the bible.
6. Establish axes: for each dominant interaction draw the line between the
   parties and name it `AXIS_<scene>_<letter>` (e.g. `AXIS_SC004_A`); record
   which side the camera lives on and where the axis may legally be re-crossed
   (on movement, on a neutral shot, or on an establishing re-orient).
7. Note entrances and exits with plan direction, feeding screen-direction
   decisions in `shot-sequencing`.
8. Verify every position is coverable from mapped angles on the chosen axis
   side; request new map angles rather than bending the blocking.

## Outputs
- `production/scenes/<SC_ID>/blocking.yaml`: positions, paths, eyelines,
  business, and axis definitions per beat.

## Quality Bar
- Every character has a position and orientation for every beat.
- Every movement has a trigger and a motivation.
- Every interaction that will get reverse coverage has a named axis and side.
- Blocking references real map zones and survives the establishing wide.

## Common Failure Modes
- Blocking in prose ("near the window") instead of plan coordinates and zones.
- Eyelines undefined, so generated close-ups look past each other.
- Axis established but re-crossed without a legal transition.
- Business invented per shot rather than blocked per beat, breaking continuity.

## Related Agents
- shot-planner
- showrunner
- cinematographer

## Related Commands
- /scene-breakdown
- /smart-shot

## Notes
Blocking is the spatial contract that `cinematography`, `shot-sequencing`, and
`continuity-checking` all audit against. Change blocking, then re-derive shots —
never the reverse.
